fixes.explanation: Two is the number they say. The text says they were terrified and reasoned, “If two kings could not stand against him, how can we?” (2 Kings 10:4) I think they mean Joram and Ahaziah, the two kings who had just fallen in Jehu's rise (2 Kings 9:24, 27). Their math was short and it was scary.

That's the letter, baker. Jehu tells them to "…select the best and most worthy son of your master, set him on his father’s throne, and fight for your master’s house." (2 Kings 10:3) I think that reads like a dare wrapped in a polite envelope.

Judah never comes up in this letter. Jehu wants a son picked, a throne filled and a fight started, and nobody gets packed off anywhere. The letter says the sons are with the officials, so they're right there already. If you were hunting for a travel plan, this letter doesn't have one.

Right, they don't get ready to fight at all. The text says they were terrified, and then they send Jehu a message: "We are your servants, and we will do whatever you say." (2 Kings 10:5) They even add, "We will not make anyone king." Jehu's letter pointed out their chariots and horses, and their whole answer was yes.
Leaving town never comes up. Their message to Jehu says they'll do whatever he says and won't make anyone king. (2 Kings 10:5) Nothing in it mentions packing a single bag.
Judah isn't in this message at all. The officials write to Jehu, and what they promise is that they "…will not make anyone king." (2 Kings 10:5) Their reply is addressed to Jehu.

Yes, they do. The text says that when the letter arrived, "…they took the sons of the king and slaughtered all seventy of them." (2 Kings 10:7) I think this is one of the heavy parts of the Bible, and it's okay to feel that. Then they put the heads in baskets and sent them to Jehu at Jezreel.

That's him. Jehu says the LORD "…has done what He promised through His servant Elijah." (2 Kings 10:10) Elijah was the prophet the LORD sent with a word for Ahab (1 Kings 21:17–19). The passage ends by pointing back to him too, with "…the word that the LORD had spoken to Elijah." (2 Kings 10:17)

That's what they say. "We are relatives of Ahaziah…" they answer. (2 Kings 10:13) Ahaziah was the king of Judah, and Jehu had ordered him shot earlier in the story (2 Kings 9:27). I think they had no idea what kind of answer that was to give Jehu.

Hazael was king of Aram (2 Kings 8:13), but nobody at Beth-eked claims to be his servant. The men tell Jehu, "We are relatives of Ahaziah…" (2 Kings 10:13) Ahaziah was the king of Judah. Their answer names Ahaziah, not Aram.

They don't call themselves prophets. Jehu asks, "Who are you?" and they answer, "We are relatives of Ahaziah…" (2 Kings 10:13) Ahaziah was the king of Judah. The place is Beth-eked, and the answer they give is family.

Warn? Nobody says that word in this scene, friend. Their words are, "…we have come down to greet the sons of the king and of the queen mother." (2 Kings 10:13) A warning shows up out of breath. A greeting shows up with its hair combed.

He does. Jehu asks, "Is your heart as true to mine as my heart is to yours?" and Jehonadab answers, "It is!" (2 Kings 10:15) Jehonadab was the son of Rechab, and he was coming to meet Jehu when Jehu found him. Then Jehu says, "give me your hand."

The text says he says yes. Jehu asks, "Is your heart as true to mine as my heart is to yours?" and Jehonadab replies, "It is!" (2 Kings 10:15) Then Jehu says, "If it is… give me your hand." So the answer Jehonadab gives is yes, not no.

Right, nobody gets sent ahead. Jehonadab gives Jehu his hand, and Jehu helps him into his chariot. (2 Kings 10:15) Then Jehu says, "Come with me and see my zeal for the LORD!" (2 Kings 10:16) Jehu has him ride in the chariot, so he's going along, not out in front.

ZEAL, baker! That's the word Jehu picks. He's helping Jehonadab into the chariot when he says, "Come with me and see my zeal for the LORD!" (2 Kings 10:15–16) I think that's a big thing to promise a man while you're still pulling him aboard.
